547.title: Bharata's journey
547.hook: a prince sets out with an army to give a crown away, and at every stop someone thinks he's come to kill
547.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often follow Bharata's road through the same stops Rama made, Guha's river and Bharadvaja's hermitage, so the two journeys mirror each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday: he refuses the prize. Bharata swore his innocence to Kausalya and gave his father the last rites.

The ministers gather and do the obvious thing: they offer Bharata the throne. He says no, in front of everyone. The eldest son is king. I'm going to the forest to bring Rama home, and if he won't come, I'll stay there in his place. Then he sets out, and not quietly. Road builders go ahead clearing a path. Behind him come the queens, the priest Vasishtha, the citizens and an army. Which, from a distance, looks exactly like what it isn't.
screen: `THE ELDEST SON IS KING.` → `ROAD BUILDERS GO AHEAD.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE AN INVASION.`

segments.voice: Watch the road, because the same scene happens three times. First, the Ganga at Shringaverapura. Guha, the boatman king who ferried Rama across, sees the army and tells his people to guard the river. Why would Bharata need soldiers, unless he means Rama harm? He meets Bharata with gifts and a careful question. Bharata answers plainly, and Guha believes him. Then Guha shows him the spot under the tree where Rama and Sita slept on a bed of grass, and tells how Lakshmana stood watch all night. Bharata sees the crushed grass and is overwhelmed. Second, Bharadvaja's hermitage, where Rama stayed too. The sage welcomes him, then asks outright: you're not here to harm an innocent man, are you? Bharata is hurt, and answers again. The sage believes him, and by the power of his austerity feeds the whole army a feast fit for the gods. Third, Chitrakoot. Lakshmana climbs a tall sal tree, sees the dust and the banners of Ayodhya, and wants to fight. Bharata has come to finish us, he says. Rama stops him. Bharata loves us more than his own life. He hasn't come for that. Three times, the same suspicion. Twice it takes a conversation to clear it. The third time, Rama doesn't need one. He already knows his brother.
screen: `GUHA GUARDS THE RIVER.` · `THE GRASS BED UNDER THE TREE.` · `BHARADVAJA ASKS OUTRIGHT.` · `LAKSHMANA UP THE SAL TREE.` · then, large: `RAMA ALREADY KNOWS HIM.`

548.title: the sandals
548.hook: two brothers argue on a mountain, each trying to give the other a kingdom
548.howItsDone: Rama's sandals, the padukas, are honored in Hindu worship and art, and Ramlila performances stage the brothers' meeting at Chitrakoot.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, he comes in love. Guha and Bharadvaja questioned Bharata; Rama never doubted him.

On Chitrakoot, two brothers have an inheritance fight that runs backward: each one is trying to give the kingdom away. Bharata reaches the hut, sees Rama in bark clothes with matted hair, and falls at his feet, unable to finish a sentence. Rama lifts him up, holds him, and asks the question Bharata has dreaded the whole road. Where is our father? Why have you left him to come here?
screen: `A FIGHT TO GIVE THINGS AWAY.` → `BHARATA AT RAMA'S FEET.` → `WHERE IS OUR FATHER?`

segments.voice: Bharata tells him. The king is dead, grieving for you. Rama falls like a cut tree. When he can stand, he goes down to the Mandakini with his brothers and Sita, and offers his father water and a ball of ingudi pulp, the forest food they've been living on. In Valmiki's telling, he says: what a person eats, their ancestors eat too. Then the arguing begins, and it goes on and on. Bharata pleads: come home, be king, I'll serve you. Counselors and priests plead. Rama's answer never changes. Our father gave his word to Kaikeyi and made a promise to me. Keeping his word is how I honor him now. Fourteen years in the forest is my part; ruling Ayodhya is yours. Bharata even threatens to sit fasting at the door of the hut until Rama gives in, and Rama gently tells him that isn't the way. Finally Bharata asks for one thing. He brings out a pair of sandals adorned with gold, and asks Rama to step into them, then give them to him. Rama does. Bharata bows to the sandals. For fourteen years, he says, these will rule. I'll live outside the city in bark and matted hair, waiting for you. And if you're not back the day after fourteen years end, I'll enter the fire. Neither brother wins the argument. Both keep their word.

549.title: the sandals
549.hook: for fourteen years, the most powerful thing in Ayodhya is a pair of shoes
549.howItsDone: Nandigrama is still visited by pilgrims near Ayodhya, and in many temples and homes Rama's sandals are honored as a sign of his presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sandals. Rama stepped into them and gave them to Bharata, and your line, both keep their word.

Bharata carries the sandals home on his head. That's how Valmiki describes it: not in a box, not under his arm, but raised on his head, the way you'd carry something sacred. The army and the mothers follow, back through the places on the road. Ayodhya, when they reach it, looks to him like a dark night without a moon. And Bharata doesn't go into the palace. He has a different plan.
screen: `THE SANDALS CARRIED ON HIS HEAD.` → `A CITY LIKE A MOONLESS NIGHT.` → `NOT THE PALACE.`

segments.voice: He goes to Nandigrama, a village just outside the city, and sets the sandals on the throne. He holds the royal umbrella over them himself. When business comes, a dispute, a gift, a decision, he lays it before the sandals first, then acts as their servant. He wears bark and matted hair, as Rama does in the forest, and sleeps on the ground. Fourteen years of ruling a kingdom and refusing to be its king. A throne with a pair of sandals on it has stayed in Hindu memory ever since: in paintings, in temple images, in the phrase people use for someone who governs in another's name. Meanwhile, on Chitrakoot, the hill no longer feels the same. Rama says it's full of memories of his mothers and his brother now, and the sages tell him demons are troubling the hermitages. So the three of them move on. They stop at the hermitage of the sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, an elderly ascetic famous for her austerity. Anasuya takes Sita aside, praises her for following her husband into the forest, and gives her a garland, ornaments, and an ointment that will never fade. Sita, in return, tells her the story of her own wedding. That's where the Ayodhya Kanda ends: a sandal on a throne, and three people walking deeper into the trees. Next, the third book. The forest.

550.title: the sages
550.hook: the third book opens in a clearing full of old ascetics, and the first thing they ask a prince in bark clothes is to be their king
550.carry: you are our king, protect us
550.howItsDone: The Aranya Kanda, the book of the forest, opens with the sages' welcome in Dandaka, and their plea for protection runs through the book.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a sandal on a throne. Bharata rules from Nandigrama as the sandals' servant, and the second book closed with Anasuya's gifts to Sita.

Aranya means forest, and the third book, the Aranya Kanda, is the book of the forest. The forest Rama walks into now is Dandaka, the great wild country south of everything he knows. It isn't empty. The first thing he sees, Valmiki says, is a ring of hermitages: little huts, fires burning for the daily offerings, grass laid out for rites, deer wandering without fear, birds everywhere. Old men and women with matted hair look up from their prayers, and come out to meet him.
screen: `ARANYA: THE FOREST.` → `DANDAKA, THE WILD SOUTH.` → `A RING OF HERMITAGES.`

segments.voice: The sages see Rama, Valmiki says, and can't stop looking at him: his build, his calm, his beauty, the bark clothes he wears like a king's robes. They bring fruit, roots and water, and give the travelers a hut to rest in. Then they say something surprising. You are our king. Whether you live in a city or a forest, you are still the king, and a king is the one who protects. We've given up the rod of punishment. We've given up anger. We live by our austerities, so we're like children in your care. Protect us. Notice what's happening. Rama has just been stripped of the crown in Ayodhya. His brother is ruling through a pair of sandals. And here, the first people he meets hand the title straight back to him. Not the palace or the throne, but the duty. The sages have chosen a life without weapons, and someone has to stand between them and the dark. Hold onto that request. Much of the forest book grows out of it: the battles, the promises, even the danger that will come to Sita. It starts here, with old people in a clearing asking a young man in bark clothes to be what he was born for.

551.title: the sages
551.hook: who were the old people living in the forest, and why had they gone there at all?
551.howItsDone: The four stages of life remain an ideal in Hindu teaching; some older Hindus today take on a simpler, more prayerful life after their working years, though few literally move to the forest.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sages of Dandaka, and your line, you are our king, protect us. They've given up the rod, and asked Rama to stand guard.

Take a retired couple: the kids are grown, there are grandchildren, the house is paid off. Today they might downsize, or travel. The old law books describe another option: go to the forest. Leave the house to your children, take a few things, and spend the rest of your life on prayer and simple living. Some readers picture the people who greeted Rama in that ring of huts this way.
screen: `THE KIDS ARE GROWN.` → `ANOTHER OPTION: THE FOREST.` → `WHO GREETED RAMA.`

segments.voice: Hindu law books describe life in four stages, called ashramas. First the student, learning. Then the householder, raising a family and working. Third, vanaprastha, literally the forest dweller. The Laws of Manu say a householder may take this step when he sees his skin wrinkled, his hair gray, and his children's children born. He can go with his wife or alone, eat what grows wild, keep the sacred fires and study. For some, a fourth stage: complete renunciation. It was an ideal, and not everyone lived it, then or now. But it gave the forest a shape. Not only wilderness: a place people went to finish their lives well. Among them were the great sages. Two words come up again and again. A rishi is a seer, one to whom sacred hymns were revealed. A muni is often explained as the silent one, whose practice includes holding back speech. What they share is tapas. The word means heat, and it's used for the discipline of austerity: fasting, standing in the sun, sitting through the cold. In the epics, tapas builds real power; a sage's blessing or curse can change a king's fate. That makes their request to Rama more striking. They aren't helpless. They've chosen not to fight. And here comes Rama, dressed just like them in bark and matted hair, but carrying a bow.

552.title: the sages
552.hook: people who own almost nothing still find a way to host three guests properly
552.howItsDone: Hindu households often welcome a guest with water, a seat and food before conversation, and the Upanishad's line atithi devo bhava, treat the guest as a god, is still quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sages, and your line, tapas, the heat of discipline. They are seers and silent ones, powerful, and choosing not to fight.

At a grandmother's house, in India and plenty of other places, a visitor's rules are old ones. You will sit. You will be given water. You will be fed, hungry or not, and you will not be allowed to help with the dishes. The sages of Dandaka own almost nothing: a hut, a water pot, the bark they wear. And the first thing they do for Rama, Sita and Lakshmana is exactly that.
screen: `YOU WILL SIT. YOU WILL BE FED.` → `THE SAGES OWN ALMOST NOTHING.` → `THEY HOST ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: In the Ramayana, hospitality is almost a rite of its own. When a guest comes to a hermitage, the hosts offer water to wash the feet, water for the hands and mouth, a seat, and food, usually fruit and roots, whatever the forest gives. The Sanskrit word for a guest is atithi. One old explanation reads it as the one who comes without a date, the visitor you didn't plan for. And the Taittiriya Upanishad gives a teacher's parting words to a student, among them a line still quoted today: treat the guest as a god. It sits beside honoring your mother, your father and your teacher. So when the sages spread grass for the travelers and bring them what they have, they aren't just being polite. They're keeping a duty as serious as their prayers. Rama spends the night, rested and honored. At sunrise he takes his leave and walks on, deeper into Dandaka. Valmiki lets you feel the change. The ring of huts falls behind. The trees close in. The forest grows dense and loud with crickets, full of wild animals, with pools half dried and no paths. The sages' welcome is the last soft place for a while. Welcome first, then the wild. Out of that thick forest, the third book's first danger is coming.
screen: `WATER, A SEAT, AND FOOD.` · `ATITHI: THE GUEST.` · `TREAT THE GUEST AS A GOD.` · `MORNING: DEEPER INTO DANDAKA.` · then, large: `THE LAST SOFT PLACE.`

553.title: Viradha
553.hook: a roar in the deep forest, and something huge snatches Sita before anyone can draw a bow
553.howItsDone: Viradha is the first danger Rama meets in the Aranya Kanda, and reciters linger on Rama's grief when Sita is seized.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last soft place. The sages hosted Rama with water, a seat and food, and at sunrise he walked into the deep forest.

The noise comes first: a roar that shakes the trees. Then the shape, tall as a hill, with a gaping mouth and a huge iron spear, and on the spear, Valmiki says, hang the animals he has killed, lions, tigers and deer. His name is Viradha. Before Rama or Lakshmana can move, he grabs Sita, lifts her, and steps back, holding her. Then he speaks, and laughs at them.
screen: `A ROAR THAT SHAKES THE TREES.` → `A SPEAR HUNG WITH ANIMALS.` → `HE GRABS SITA.`

segments.voice: Viradha mocks them. You look like ascetics, with your bark and matted hair, but you carry bows and you have a woman with you. What kind of hermits are you? She'll be my wife now. And he adds: Brahma gave me a boon. No weapon can kill me. Rama's first response is grief. He turns to Lakshmana, stricken: seeing Sita in a stranger's grip hurts more than his father's death, more than losing the kingdom. It's Lakshmana, furious, who pulls him back into the moment. Both brothers shoot. Arrows strike Viradha again and again and don't kill him. He drops Sita, seizes the two brothers, swings them onto his shoulders like children, and runs off into the forest, Sita screaming after them. And the brothers, carried along, do the only thing left. They break his arms, Rama the right, Lakshmana the left. Viradha falls. So the week ends. Bharata suspected on the road. Sandals stepped into on Chitrakoot. A throne at Nandigrama with no king on it, and Anasuya's gifts. Sages asking for a protector, the heat of tapas, a guest welcomed as a god. And today the welcome ends, and the forest shows its teeth.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF HERMITS ARE YOU?` · `NO WEAPON CAN KILL ME.` · `CARRIED OFF ON HIS SHOULDERS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE FOREST SHOWS ITS TEETH.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment when something sudden happened, a shock, a bad phone call, a near miss, and you froze; let the memory be there without replaying it, and send a slow breath to wherever your body tightened. Rama froze in grief and his brother called him back, so imagine someone you trust saying your name, steady, calling you back into the room.
Viradha. The forest giant who seizes Sita, mocks the brothers as false hermits, and can't be killed by weapons.
